analysis.investment_thesis: MTAR Technologies fails both legs of the Magic Formula spectacularly: earnings yield of ~0.8% (EBIT ₹121 Cr / EV ₹15,127 Cr) signals extreme overvaluation, while ROIC of ~13% sits well below my 20% threshold. With net profit declining from ₹103 Cr (FY23) to ₹53 Cr (FY25) even as revenue grew, the business is becoming less profitable as it scales — the opposite of a quality compounder.
key_strengths: Niche defense/space/nuclear precision engineering with genuine barriers to entry and captive government clients
Revenue CAGR of 25.9% (FY20–25) shows real top-line demand from ISRO, DRDO, and clean energy programs
Gross margin of 48.8% indicates pricing power on specialized components
key_risks: Earnings yield ~0.8% — Magic Formula requires >12%; paying 226x P/E for a company with declining profits is speculative
Net profit dropped 49% from FY23 peak (₹103 Cr → ₹53 Cr in FY25) while revenue grew — severe margin compression and cost absorption
Free cash flow deeply negative for 4 of last 5 years; annual capex ~₹100 Cr consumes essentially all operating earnings, leaving zero true FCF
red_flags: Earnings yield 0.8% vs. Magic Formula minimum of 12% — 15x overvalued on this metric alone
EBITDA peaked at ₹168 Cr in FY23 and has since regressed to ₹120 Cr in FY25 — earnings power is deteriorating, not growing
Finance cost CAGR of 34.5% vs. net profit CAGR of 11.3% — debt servicing is eating shareholder returns
ROE of only 7.39% on a stock trading at 20x book — capital is being destroyed in value terms
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula: EBIT (FY25) = ₹121 Cr. EV = Market Cap ₹14,952 Cr + Net Debt ₹175 Cr = ₹15,127 Cr. Earnings Yield = 0.80%. That's not a rounding error — you are earning less than a savings account yield on the enterprise's operating earnings. On Return on Capital, using capital employed (Equity ₹744 Cr + Debt ₹177 Cr = ₹921 Cr): ROIC ≈ 13%, confirmed by management's own ROCE of 10.4%. Both numbers fail my thresholds of >12% earnings yield and >20% ROIC. The business is not cheap, and it is not exceptional enough at the current capital base to justify the premium.

The deeper problem is deteriorating profitability. MTAR's FY23 EBITDA of ₹168 Cr has shrunk to ₹120 Cr in FY25 despite revenue rising from ₹574 Cr to ₹676 Cr — operating leverage is running in reverse. High capex (₹91–108 Cr annually) for capacity expansion has not yet translated into earnings uplift, and finance costs are compounding at 34.5% annually. The stock may have a compelling long-term story in India's defense and space ecosystem, but at 226x trailing P/E and an earnings yield of sub-1%, the Magic Formula says walk away — the market has priced in decades of perfection into a business that is currently shrinking its earnings.
